title: Forgetting in prayer
hookLine: two prostrations at the end if you forget

lines: THE MAN WITH THE LONG HANDS.
cards: An afternoon prayer in Medina. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ leads it, and ends it after two units. A four-unit prayer, finished at two.

He goes and leans against a piece of wood in the mosque. People stand around, uneasy. Then a man the companions nicknamed Dhul-Yadayn, the one with the long hands, asks: has the prayer been shortened, or did you forget?
Neither, as far as he knows, he answers, and he turns to the others. Is it true? It's true.
So he goes back, prays what he left out, and adds today's word at the end.

teach.b: Sujud al-sahw means the prostrations of forgetfulness: two extra prostrations near the end of the prayer, made when something was added, left out, or is in doubt. First, that story, from Sahih al-Bukhari.
Nobody was shamed. The prayer wasn't thrown out. The missing units were prayed, and two prostrations mended it.
Second, what the Prophet said about himself. Another report in Bukhari has him say, after a slip in prayer: I am only a human being like you.
I forget as you forget. So when I forget, remind me. That line comes from the one who had just led the prayer.
Third, doubt. A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives a familiar case: you can't remember whether you've prayed three units or four.

teach.h: BUILD ON WHAT YOU'RE SURE OF.
teach.b: Throw the doubt away, it says, and build on what you're sure of, then make two prostrations before you finish. Not start over. Not stand there replaying it.
Fourth, where the schools differ: whether the two prostrations come before the closing salam or after it.

The Hanafi school places them after. The Shafi'i school places them before. The Maliki school depends on whether something was added or left out, and the Hanbali school follows the specific report for each case.
They agree on the main thing: the prayer comes with its own repair kit.

how: When Muslims add to, leave out, or lose count in a prayer, they make two extra prostrations near its end, before or after the closing salam depending on their school, and the prayer stands.

o: a prayer of repentance made after a serious sin
starting the whole prayer over after any mistake
two prostrations near the end of prayer that mend a slip

games.q: forgetting in prayer — tap the pairs.
p: so when I forget, remind me
build on what you're sure of

s: the Prophet never made a mistake in prayer
Bukhari reports him saying: I am only a human being like you. I forget as you forget.
if you lose count, the hadith says build on what you're sure of
Sahih Muslim: throw the doubt away, build on certainty, then two prostrations.
every school places the two prostrations in the same spot
the Hanafi school puts them after the salam, the Shafi'i before, and others depend on the case.

games.q: you're in the row. the Prophet ends a four-unit prayer after two. people look at each other. you have long hands and a nickname to match. what do you do?
o: say nothing: he must know best.
ask: was the prayer shortened, or did you forget?
leave and pray it again alone.
games.why: Dhul-Yadayn asked. the others confirmed it, and the Prophet prayed what was missing and added two prostrations (Sahih al-Bukhari).

practice: Bring to mind one small mistake from this week, a forgotten call, a missed step, a word in the wrong place, and see it without replaying it; then picture one small step that would mend it, and let the replaying go on the out-breath.
If you pray, remember the two prostrations next time you lose count, and mend the prayer rather than abandon it. If you don't, simply set the mistake down, and leave it there.

wordCard.voice: Sujud al-sahw. The prostrations of forgetfulness: two prostrations near the end of the prayer that mend a slip. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the prostrations of forgetfulness. sahw is an oversight, a slip of attention.

carryVoice: Your line: mistakes are expected. Even the Prophet said: I forget as you forget. Same time tomorrow.
